newsitem.title: USA: Engineers seek leak on U.S. shuttle.
newsitem.headline: Engineers seek leak on U.S. shuttle.

text.p: NASA engineers preparing shuttle Discovery for launch on a mission to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, searched on Sunday for the source of an oxygen leak.
Space agency officials said they were optimistic the problem would not delay Discovery's planned 3:55 a.m. EST (0855 GMT) blastoff on Tuesday.

High concentrations of the gas were detected in the shuttle's cargo bay and fuselage after Discovery was loaded with supercold liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen for its electricity-generating fuel cells.
Engineers hoped a leaky connector in the launch pad equipment was responsible and not a problem with the shuttle's complex fuel cell system which lies beneath the shuttle's cargo bay.
A team was being dispatched to the launch pad on Sunday to investigate the problem, NASA test director Doug Lyons said at a news conference.
"Depending on what they find, there may have to be some more extensive work done," he said.
Launch controllers also faced another hurdle with the shuttle's fuel cells. They said it would be Monday before they could check whether one of three devices was working properly.
Air force meteorologists gave Discovery a 70 percent chance of fair weather for its predawn blastoff from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.
The shuttle was to rendezvous with the Hubble Space Telescope two days later to install new scientific instruments and upgrade various ageing components.
The telescope's fragile solar panels were expected to make the astronauts' maintenance work tricky, but astronomers said the risks were out weighed by the scientific rewards.
It would be the first time astronauts have visited the telescope since a 1993 repair mission corrected its blurred vision.
